title: Anathapindika
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett tells the story of Anathapindika, the Buddha's great donor, reading from a mashup of Pali sutras and Wikipedia just as a fundraising campaign approaches. Anathapindika meets the Buddha in the dark before dawn, buys Prince Jeta's park by covering it in coins, loses his fortune to a flood, and evicts a deva who urges him to stop giving. Near death, Anathapindika hears Shariputra and Ananda teach on impermanence and asks that such teachings be given to lay people too. Nomon then plays a Thich Nhat Hanh Q&A on the deathbed scene, where recollecting the Three Jewels waters seeds of happiness, and ends wondering about Visakha, the female patron the sources barely describe.

He was born with the given name Sudhata, and he was the son of a wealthy merchant named Sumana.
He was also a relative of Subhuti, who you may have heard of, who later became an important disciple of the Buddha.
When Sudhata, who became Anathapindika when Sudhata grew up, married, he married a woman named Twinyalakana, the sister of a wealthy merchant in Rajagaha.

Sudhata was known for his generosity, even before his conversion to Buddhism, and was known to the public by this name Anathapindika, which means one who gives alms to the unprotected, due to his love for giving.
Anathapindika had a family, a son and three daughters.
So, not unlike society of today, some things are just perennial in human culture.
His family was wealthy and he himself was skilled with wealth.
And we also know this is a time in India with kind of an emergence of a merchant class and an increase in reliance on cash economy, moving beyond barter economy and simple agrarian economy.
So he also was born into a time when wealth was possible, great wealth was becoming more possible.
One day while traveling and in business, Anathapindika went to visit his brother-in-law, who was already a follower of the Buddha.
When he arrived at his brother-in-law's house, he noticed that the household was preparing for an elaborate feast.
He figured that was preparation for a wedding or a visit from the king.
When Anathapindika asked about these preparations, his brother-in-law explained that they were preparing for a visit from the Buddha, from the awakened one and his monks.
Anathapindika had never heard about this yet.
Hearing this, he was overjoyed, saying, "You mean that a fully enlightened being has arisen in the world?
Wow."
And he immediately resolved to go meet him.
So it must have been part of the general educated worldview that even before there was Buddhism, there could be enlightened beings born into the world.
Sometimes they were in the world and sometimes they weren't.
So maybe there's one in the world now.
The following day, Anathapindika rose early to meet the Buddha.

It was too early to go meet anybody.
But he continued on his way, and then a friendly yaka spirit whispered in his ear and urged him to continue.
Anathapindika eventually approached a figure, a dim figure in the dark, who called out to him, "Sudhata," and asked him to come forward.
He was really surprised because nobody really knew his birth name.
He wasn't known by that.
He was always known as Anathapindika, this honorific for being so generous.
So he concluded this could only be this awakened one.
This could only be the Buddha.
And he went forward.

Just right off the bat, he entered the state of Sotapanna, the stage of enlightenment.

So, yeah, he was convinced he had found a great teacher.
Following his first encounter with the Buddha, he requested to offer him regular meals, the Buddha and his monks, which he accepted.
Then he asked the Buddha if he could build a temple for his monks in his hometown of Savatthi, to which the Buddha agreed.
OK, so now he goes to Savatthi and he's looking around.
He wants to find a good place, a really propitious place to build this new practice center, to build this new monastery.
He was looking for a place that was accessible to the followers, but also peaceful and secluded, not too far away, not too close.
Eventually he came across a beautiful forested park, on the edge of town or something, belonging to Prince Jetta, who was the son of King Pasanadi of Kosala.
So Anathapindika made an appointment and went to talk to the prince and asked about buying the park.
But the prince refused.
He really loved his park.
He had no interest in selling.
Why would you sell your royal park, I guess, if you're a prince?
You don't need money, probably.
But Anathapindika really persisted.
He kept at it.
And so the prince, finally in exasperation, said, "OK, I'll sell you the park if you cover it completely in coins."
Every square inch covered with money, with coins.
Thinking, what a ridiculous thing, impossible, a good way to get rid of this guy.
And to the prince's great surprise, Anathapindika agreed to this price.
Then the prince said, "No, I wasn't serious, I don't want to sell the park."
He's just giving you shit.
So Anathapindika said, "No, no, no, you made an agreement."
They went to the royal arbitrators, who concluded that Prince Jedha had agreed and made an offer, had named his price to sell the park at this price.
And so Anathapindika sent to all his people, sent to the banks and to his people.
Wagon loads and wagon loads of money were hauled to the park by oxen, probably.
He and all his helpers set about covering the land with coins.
They had enough coins to cover all but one little area kind of near the entrance to the new monastery.
Anathapindika was about to order another wagon load when the prince jumped in and said, "No, no, no, I'm so impressed with your resolve and your dedication to this Buddha.
I'll fill out the rest of it."
So Prince Jedha donated the rest of the land.
He also offered to build a wall and a gate and to provide trees for timber.
Even after that, Anathapindika made many more donations to build temple and temple and huts and furnishings and stuff.
None of this survives archaeologically, so we have no idea from our modern realist perspective exactly how elaborate the place was.
Temple could mean lots of things.
But there are some structures.
You kind of get the impression the Buddha always sat outside under a tree, but actually he made use of buildings too.
Mostly they would make use of buildings during the rainy period and the summer monsoons, when you can't really sit outside, even if you're the Buddha.
But the rest of the dry parts of the year, I think they did sleep outside, camp outside.
Anyway, Anathapindika built this monastery.

One scholar, trying to analyze the economics of the day and trying to understand the units that are mentioned in the original stories, estimated that Anathapindika spent about three-fifths of his total fortune to set this up.
This place became known as Jetavana, Jeta's Wood or Jeta's Grove.
The temple itself is often referred to as Anathapindika's monastery in Jeta's Woods, to give recognition to both benefactors.
The Buddha was so moved that he designated Anathapindika as his chief patron, along with a woman named Visakha.
Anathapindika was then considered to be the male Buddhist lay disciple foremost in generosity.
The texts relate that he kept at it.
He regularly sent food, medicine and supplies to Jetavana and received monks at his house for alms and support of the sangha every way he could.
He also sent workers and servants to help maintain the monastery.
When he went away from home, he would send his eldest daughter, so she also became a great practitioner.

Anathapindika soundly beats the followers of this other tradition.

Anathapindika and Visakha were not only these great donors, but they were also his primary aides.

It wasn't in a bank, it was buried somewhere or something.

White-clad lay followers are serious lay followers who wear a white practice robe, but they're not ordained.
Such profound talk will not be clear for them, not clear for white-clad lay followers, clear only for ascetics, for monastics.
*And Anathapindika answered, "Venerable Shariputra, let such talks on the Dharma be given to the white-clad laity too.
There are those with just a little dust in their eyes.
If they don't hear these teachings, they will be lost.
Some may be able to understand, as I have."*
